$comment: What this repository contributes to a running stack, and what a check may
believe about it. `checked` is proved against this repository by
internal/manifest/manifest_test.go in this repository's own CI; `declared` is
a statement nobody can verify and carries its own `why`.
THE FACT WORTH DECLARING HERE IS THE EXIT-CODE CONTRACT, BECAUSE ANOTHER
REPOSITORY READS IT. stack-up's routine dispatches on it: 0 is ok, 1 is
findings, and anything else is an error the operator is shown. So the
difference between `I would not start` and `I ran and it went badly` is a
cross-repository interface, not an implementation detail, and it is checked
here by running the binary at each of them.
2  refused for configuration, before contacting anything
1  ran the drill and scenarios failed
0  ran the drill and everything held
It refuses at three separate points and all three are exit 2: no scenario
directory, no gateway, and a scenario that declares expect.event with no
event log to watch. The third still refuses when a gateway IS configured,
which is what makes this fail-before-half-the-job rather than fail-fast.
`report` is a subcommand of the same binary and is NOT declared as a
component. It is what a human runs afterwards over a saved report, not
something a deployment installs, and inventing a component name no launcher
uses would put a name into this estate that nothing means.

report_is_the_human_half.why: The same binary, read afterwards by a person over a report the drill wrote. No launcher installs or schedules it, so it is not a component here. It refuses with the same exit 2 when given no file.

the_scenarios_ship_in_this_repository.why: stack-up points the routine at its own checkout of this repository and stack-k8s mounts them at /scenarios. Which scenarios a deployment chooses to run is its decision, so the count is not checked here.
